results.draft_locus: Concepts: Four Things That Must Stay Apart ¶1
results.quote: The single place Ingrid asks for is not one system. The chapter's core decision is to keep four concerns apart, a separation most marketplaces reach only after the spaghetti:
results.finding: The four-concerns table (question answered, when it changes, owner, must not contain) is introduced only by 'keep four concerns apart' and is followed directly by the delivery-evidence paragraph. No sentence says what the table shows: that each concern changes for its own reasons and has its own owner, which is why merging any two fails. The spec's controlling idea for p09 names exactly those points.

All other evidence is explained: the price-dimensions table (framed by 'A price is a function, not a field'), the ledger-entry table and Figure 3 (explained by 'The current balance of any entitlement is the sum of its entries'), the paid-fields table, the enforcement-point table ('the right-hand column of the table is a commercial decision'), the feed-policy table ('Any of the four can be right'), the public-record table, the trade-offs, verticals and matrix tables, and the Rightmove, Vinted, Autotrader, CarGurus, Stripe and Adevinta quotations each have a sentence saying what they show.

Every declared transition_in was read at its boundary and is expressed: e.g. 'Felix Brandt ... It turns out to be structural' (cause_effect), 'alongside a second agenda item' (additional_support), 'The single place Ingrid asks for is not one system' (problem_solution), 'Two design rules follow' (cause_effect), 'The two paths should share ... and nothing else' (contrast), 'Any of the four can be right, but three rules are not optional' (contrast), 'That gap shapes the build-or-buy decision' (cause_effect), 'Under Tally, Ruhrblick's August invoice would carry no overage line' (problem_solution), 'The trade-offs hold in every vertical, but each has its own hardest problem' (elaboration), 'Decisions above any one team prevent these failures' (problem_solution), the bold failure-mode lead-in phrases (additional_support, phrase), and 'One family of paid products still needs its own machinery' (contrast to the hand-off). The deterministic hand-off link check passes.

Both flow readers describe the declared organising principle (problem → concepts → the core in the order of a sale → public record → replay of the scene → application), name a reason for every section's position, and say the overall order needs no change. Both also flagged Common Ground, Ghost Inventory, Search as System of Record and the March 2027 neutrality decision / 'share platforms, not products' (A2/B1, A4/B2, A8/B6) as unexplained; these are not counted as failures because the spec's audience.already_knows lists Common Ground and those failure-pattern names, and the neutrality decision and the slogan are introduced in earlier chapters (e.g. sellers-and-accounts, listing-ingestion) the target reader has read.

results.quote: Figure 2 lays the four concerns along a sale: the catalog and price lists define, the pricing engine sells, the ledger holds, the delivery systems deliver and emit delivery evidence, and billing settles.
results.finding: Both readers stopped here: the figure has five stages while the sentence speaks of four concerns, and the fifth stage (delivery systems) is not one of the four concerns, so the reader has to work out the mapping. Reader A: 'The figure caption says "five stages". It took a moment to see that the delivery systems are the fifth stage.' The spec order is fine; the prose should say that the four concerns plus the delivery systems make five stages.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B3 ('The figure also says "five stages" while the text says "four concerns", so I had to stop and work out how the two map onto each other.')

results.draft_locus: Architecture: The Commercial Core ¶9 (enforcement-point table, feed-import row)
results.quote: apply the contract's overflow policy once the quota effect is current
results.finding: The feed-import row of the enforcement-point table uses 'the contract's overflow policy' before 'Quotas meet feeds' introduces the four overflow policies, so both readers met it as an unexplained forward reference. The spec's chronological order (enforcement points, then feeds as the hardest case) is sound; the cell should point forward explicitly or describe the behavior without the undefined term. (Quoted from the table attached to this unit, as both readers quote it.)
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B4 ('the feed-import row says "apply the contract's overflow policy." Overflow policies are introduced only in the next subsection')

results.quote: Its evidence column names the delivery events and ledger entries that reconciliation compares.
results.finding: The matrix's evidence column uses SlotConsumed, BoostExecuted and LeadDelivered (and a 'Motorvane lead allowance (pilot)' row) while the ledger table and the worked example name entries Consume and PublishRefused and events ListingPaidEffectChanged and AccountQuotaChanged; neither reader could tell whether these are new events or other names for the same ones. The prose should say which are ledger entries and which are delivery events, or use the names already introduced.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B10 ('It is unclear whether SlotConsumed is the same thing as a Consume entry or a different event.')

results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B9 ('The first failure is fused into the intro sentence, where every other failure starts its own paragraph.')

All other chapter-owned terms are given at or before first use: product catalog, pricing engine, entitlement, quota, effect and enforcement point (Introduction ¶2), delivery evidence (Concepts ¶2), effect projector (Architecture ¶6), overage (scene ¶1), proration (glossed in Architecture ¶1), revenue recognition over the display period and variable consideration (Architecture ¶15), CPQ (In Practice ¶3).

The introduction opens from the prior chapter and a direct-statement hook ('A seller who paid for a "Top listing" and never appeared on top ... is a customer the marketplace has wronged'), defines its terms, labels its evidence and gives a roadmap; none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, dawn-of-man or book report.

The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic or evidence (the advertising paragraph is the declared hand-off), and does not end on a rephrased thesis alone; none of the four weak types.

From Products to Attention ¶1 joins what no single section states: the same ledger records the 150 consumptions and 13 refused publications, receives the price-list release, feeds ranking's paid fields and is what reconciliation checks; so-what: 'A group that builds it once changes prices as data and proves every invoice line; one that leaves package checks scattered learns of its errors from dealers.'

The conclusion returns to the declared callback: 'Ruhrblick's €117 and the price-event estimate had one cause, and one record answers both', closing both scene problems with the ledger, the projection and the reconciliation.

The intro-only reader predicted the sections in order (invoice and price event, four concerns, the core in sale order with ledger, effects, enforcement points, feeds, billing, sold versus delivered, public record, replay of both cases, trade-offs, verticals, failure modes, Chief Architect's view, questions), the evidence (investor results, billing-vendor documentation, EU rules, the fictional case, labelled a reference-architecture inference) and the declarative, prescriptive tone.

Matches AC-2's expected answer: the commercial core and the sold-versus-delivered test, the four terms, the reference-architecture inference, the full section sequence and the evidence kinds (dated investor sources, vendor documentation, EU law, fictional Veldmark).

Matches AC-1's expected answer: no single record of what can be sold, held and delivered; catalog, pricing engine, append-only ledger with idempotency keys and refused publications, and billing kept apart, so Ruhrblick is billed from 150 consumptions with no overage; effects projected to fast read models; daily reconciliation; prices as reviewed, reversible catalog/price-list releases.

Matches AC-4's expected answer: 31,000 qps × ~400 candidates ≈ 12 million answers a second; effect projector writes paid.* fields onto the listing document; bounded staleness, index never the record, re-projected on rebuild; projector consumes lifecycle events and sold/removed listings carry no paid fields, else Ghost Inventory with a price tag.

Matches AC-5's expected answer: paid consumer publication fails closed (free fails open); feed import queues and retries, never skips silently, reports to the feed; ranking serves last projected effects logged as stale; fail-open default documented per enforcement point; the overflow policy is a contract term stored with the entitlement, each refused car gets a PublishRefused entry and a feed-report line, and billing counts published listings from the ledger.
